text: Pain Reprocessing Therapy's first big trial was only in mild to moderate chronic back pain. There, 66% of the people who got four weeks of the therapy rated their pain 0 or 1 out of 10 afterward, compared to 20% of those given a placebo shot, and the gains mostly held a year later.
reader: an adult whose pain has lasted months with no injury or disease found to explain it, who came to the guide partly for that pain, deciding whether one of two pain therapies fits them, and which

sentences.s: Pain Reprocessing Therapy's first big trial was only in mild to moderate chronic back pain.
sentences.payoff: they learn the evidence is only for mild to moderate back pain, so they know how far it reaches their pain
sentences.follows: it turns from what the therapy is to its evidence, limit first

sentences.s: There, 66% of the people who got four weeks of the therapy rated their pain 0 or 1 out of 10 afterward, compared to 20% of those given a placebo shot, and the gains mostly held a year later.
sentences.payoff: they learn how many ended up nearly pain-free, against placebo, and that it lasted
sentences.follows: it gives the result of the trial just named

checked.point: 66% vs 20% at 0 or 1 out of 10 after 4 weeks, largely maintained at a year; mild or moderate pain
checked.found: Ashar et al. 2022, JAMA Psychiatry 79(1):13-23 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8482298); NIH Research Matters, 2021-11-02 (https://www.nih.gov/news-events/nih-research-matters/retraining-brain-treat-chronic-pain)
checked.still_needed: yes: they weigh it for their own pain

placement: after what the therapy is, before the second therapy

opens.first_sentence: Pain Reprocessing Therapy's first big trial was only in mild to moderate chronic back pain.
opens.why_reading: it says whether the evidence covers their kind of pain

same_point: none: read the section from its heading to the next; the EAET evidence is the fifth paragraph, about another therapy

marked.s: Its first big trial was only in chronic back pain, and there 66% were pain-free or nearly so after four weeks of it, against 20% given a placebo shot, with the gains mostly holding a year later.
marked.difference: 1, 4, 9, 10: one sentence carrying the trial's limit, two percentages, the placebo comparison, the four weeks and the follow-up; "nearly so" is vague; "four weeks of it" could mean the therapy or the pain. His way

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
